doc.title: Jim Cullum interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Fantasies about Bix Beiderbecke's last years and Teagarden's praise
summary: Cullum imagines helping Bix and relays Teagarden saying nothing matched hearing Beiderbecke live.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: But if you’d like to ask me what else I would like to do, that I’ve fantasized about, you know there are all kinds of things with Beiderbecke that I’ve fantasized about. Beiderbecke died in Queens and he died a tragic, down and out situation you know. His last year he was just around and Teagarden said that in the recording studio they would try to record and he overheard him, kind of eerie, talk to the cornet and say, “Don’t let me down, don’t let me down today” you know. And this guy, he started having trouble playing you know, having trouble, problems, physical problems. But I’ve thought about going to and knocking on his door you know, knocking on this door and seeing this bleary eyed guy come out and say, “Say, let me see if I can’t be of some help to you.” You know? And I’ve thought about that. I thought about hearing him play in his prime, which a lot of people did. I thought about just going around and hearing him play. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -17-

Because the people that heard him a lot, Teagarden told me this, said that there was never any experience that he ever had in music like hearing Beiderbecke play live. It was — the records never quite got it. And there was never anything like it. Teagarden said, “I think he was the greatest artist that there ever was in history.” Teagarden was such a nut about Beiderbecke. He was just a — and Teagarden was a great admirer of many other players too, and particularly Armstrong. He had heard Armstrong when he was a very young guy and Teagarden was real young, he was only about 17 years old and went to New Orleans and heard Louis play over there. And he was fascinated all the rest of his life. But he said there was just nothing like hearing Beiderbecke play live, the sound and all the passion and everything that was in that thing was so compelling.
